name: Sam Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the office side at a haulage depot, a family firm with about twenty lorries on an industrial estate outside town. I file the delivery notes the drivers bring back, sort out the shift sheets, chase missing paperwork and answer the phone when a customer wants to know where their pallet is. Most of it's still paper, which I don't mind. Gary, the owner's son, runs the yard and he's my boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know where everything is, in the grey cabinets behind my desk. What wears me out is the drivers who hand in crumpled notes with coffee on them at half five. I live with my girlfriend Hannah, who works the tills at the supermarket, and there's not much left over at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, more or less. People get excited about every new gadget. At the depot nobody would care, they'd be talking about fuel prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job as it is, which is what I want. I don't use any of these AI things and I'm not keen to start. The real worry is whether the firm itself keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on. Maybe I'd finally learn the proper tracking system Gary keeps nagging me about, because that's not going away. And I'd try not to put the car on the credit card again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Not worried about robots, worried about the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most of it's still paper. Would anything at the depot change at all here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe some tracking program does the phone calls about where the pallet is. That'd be a quarter of my day gone, to be fair. I'd hope Gary keeps me on for the filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money worry that's there anyway, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel's up, and we lost a big supermarket contract last spring. If the haulage firm loses one more big contract, Gary (my boss) will cut the office before he cuts a single driver.

At the depot people would just keep talking about **fuel prices**.
think: Privately I'm glad my **job stays** as it is.
The real worry is whether the **firm itself** keeps going.
do: Learn the **tracking system** Gary keeps nagging me about.
Stop putting **car costs** on the credit card before the overdraft fills up.
feel: **Fine** about robots, but worried about the **bills**.
S0.quote: If the haulage firm loses one more big contract, Gary (my boss) will cut the office before he cuts a single driver.
fieldNote: Sam is relieved by the plateau but the **firm's finances** worry him already.
He notices that even small AI could take the **pallet calls**, a quarter of his day.
He expects the **office** to be cut before drivers.

steps.text: Learn the depot's tracking system this winter
Stop putting car repairs on the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for a firm like ours, we're too small. I'd probably say it to Gary too, half hoping he agrees. Online I don't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the shift sheets and the paperwork are exactly what these programs do. The drivers still need to drive, for a while. I'm the easy saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do whatever course Gary asked, even though I'd hate it. I'd ask if I could do some yard work as well, checking loads, so I'm not only office. And we'd stop eating out completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I don't like change at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Gary's the one who'd decide. What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gary straight: I know where every bit of paper is, and the program won't. I've kept the haulage firm's paperwork straight for two years, and a computer won't know which driver always loses the delivery notes. Not sure he'd care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hannah cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract and the Friday pizza. Then the gym, which I don't use much anyway. Hannah would want to keep the holiday money, and we'd argue about it.

Cut the **phone contract** and Friday pizza.
feel: **Sick**, because he dislikes change at the best of times.
S1.quote: I've kept the haulage firm's paperwork straight for two years, and a computer won't know which driver always loses the delivery notes.
fieldNote: Sam's public line is **denial**, but privately he names himself the easy saving.
He'd move toward **hands-on yard work**, sensing robots come later.
His only real asset is **knowing the firm**, and he doubts Gary values it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it won't happen that fast, because I wouldn't want to believe it. If it did, I'd say the government has to do something. I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at the depot. I don't know computers and I don't know anything else. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary to keep me in the yard, and I'd ask my uncle about his removals business. Past that, I don't have a plan. We've got about three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, to be honest. Like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come around three years later. Does the yard work buy you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if Gary keeps me on. Loading lorries in the rain might keep me working until 2031, and that's the best plan I've got. After that I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hannah we'd have to move in with her parents. She wouldn't love it. We'd be back in her old bedroom at twenty-seven.

say: I'd say it **won't happen** that fast, because I wouldn't want to believe it.
If it did, the **government** has to act.
think: Privately I'd be **finished** at the depot.
I don't know computers or **anything else**, so I wouldn't know where to start.
do: Ask Gary to move me to **yard work**.
Ask my uncle about his **removals business**.
Move in with **Hannah's parents** to save rent.
S2.quote: Loading lorries in the rain might keep me working until 2031, and that's the best plan I've got.
fieldNote: Sam has **no plan** beyond the yard and family, with three weeks of savings.
He sees the **robot delay** as a short reprieve for hands-on yard work.
Moving in with **Hannah's parents** would feel like a step backwards.

steps.text: Ask Gary to move me to full-time yard work
Ask my uncle for work in his removals business
Move in with Hannah's parents to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, it'll be slower than they say. But I'd probably admit at work that we should all think about it. Gary might even put on a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd have time to get something in my hands. Not sure what. I'm still not a computer person and I won't pretend to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the lorry licence, since the firm sometimes pays for it. I'd try to save something, even fifty a month. And I'd stay at the depot as long as there's a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but less like the floor's gone. More like it's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, actually, because the robots don't drive until about 2034 on that card. With a lorry licence I'd be driving for seven years instead of filing for three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about getting a lorry licence yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary's dad paid for two of the lads' licences last year. It's a few thousand. I'd have to ask, which I hate doing.

say: I'd still say it'll be **slower** than they say.
At work I'd admit we should all **think about it**.
think: Privately five years gives me time to get something **hands-on**.
I'm still **not a computer person** and won't pretend.
do: Ask the firm to pay for a **lorry licence**.
Stay at the depot **desk** as long as it lasts.
feel: **Scared**, but more like tilting than falling.
S3.quote: With a lorry licence I'd be driving for seven years instead of filing for three.
fieldNote: The extra time makes Sam think of a **lorry licence**, using the robot delay.

He still expects to **lose the desk job**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, plenty of time to sort it out. I'd probably not think about it much until it got close. That's just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know I'd leave it too late. But ten years is enough to get a licence, drive a few years, and maybe save a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the lorry licence in the next couple of years, when I'm ready. I'd keep the office job meanwhile. Honestly I'd probably wait and see for the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. Worried, but I can push it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that enough for someone who doesn't like change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I start in year five, no. If I start now, maybe. I know myself, and I'd still be filing delivery notes in 2035 thinking there's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hannah's family are here, my mum's here. I'd rather do a worse job here than a better one two hundred miles away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and no savings and nothing but paper skills. What would help is the firm paying for a licence, or some government scheme that pays you while you learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what happens to small firms. Big companies will buy the robots first, and little depots like ours will just close instead of changing.

headlineQuote: Big companies will buy the robots first, and little depots like ours will just close instead of changing.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** office administrator at a family haulage depot.
He keeps **paper files** and avoids AI tools entirely.
He lives with Hannah, a **supermarket** worker, on very little savings.
He swings from anxious in the plateau to **panicked** under AGI by 2028.
His only plan is **hands-on work** in the yard or a lorry licence.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with two years, no savings and only paper skills.
whatWouldHelp: A firm-paid **lorry licence** or a scheme that pays him while learning a **trade**.
